_comment: Barnaby, Chapters Two to Four: the codes, Pell's name, the lift he won't ride, the news about Wren, the reunion or the grief, and what the Heart needs from him.

lines.text: The winch is singing. Cable's taking the cage's weight down there in the dark. I could hear it from the annex. I went and stood next to it for an hour, which is not the same as getting in.
No. I'm not getting in it. You know why. If you find them, knock. I'll be by the gauge, pretending to read it.
She told me to stop that face. I said I'd stop when she stopped coughing. She laughed until she coughed. We're both very stubborn and only one of us is right.
I read the journal on the lift up. All the way. The cage stopped and I stayed in it. Eleven years, and every page starts with my initial. I don't know what to do with being remembered that hard.
Damp season. The lake breathes out and the children breathe in. Same every year. Odile counts the coughs. I count the pipes that sweat. Nobody counts the moss, except Hesper, who's right to.
Tolley? Tolley Brand? Down there? He owes me a spanner. I mean: good. Good that he's alive. Also the spanner.
Tolley's back on the Lease cot. He brought me a spanner. Not mine. Better than mine. I've never been so annoyed to be given something.
Knock at Hush, from the pipe-heads in the lane. If the answer comes, write it down before you decide what it means.
The gauge reads two-point-eight now. Somebody below is pushing back. I stare at it so you don't have to.

Crew cable: four moss fibre, two brass, plaited tight. Two lengths for the drum. Fit them through the glass, under the pump hall. Then feed it thirty power, on its own wire. One wire carries sixty and the pump eats fifty-five of it. Then don't look down.
Take a respirator. Take a lens. Take somebody's word that you'll come back, and keep it.
Hands are steadier in the mornings now. I'm blaming the tea. I'm told that's cowardly.
She's still talking. I can tell from here.

codes.say: I've been up all night with the gauge. It moved twice. There's pressure on the far side, and someone leaning on it.
You want to answer them. You've got a face like a dropped spanner.
Crew code. Wren and I wrote half of it on a bet. Write this down.
Three-two-three: still here. One-one: yes. Two-two: no. Four: come. Three-three: bad air. One-two-one: how many. Two-one-two: who. Five: help.
Letters are a tap for the row and a tap for the column. Nobody uses letters. Letters are for when you've run out of everything else.
The pipe-heads in the lane go down to the Trunk the long way round. Knock at Hush, when Wick's own water goes quiet. Answers take a day.
No. ...Not yet. If it's someone who knows the code, they'll know my hand. I'm not ready to be known.
Then it's a very polite pipe, and I'll owe it an apology.

pell_name.say: Not a crew name. Not one of ours. Trunk crew were thirty-one people and I knew all their names, and the names of their cats.
Which means somebody taught a stranger the code. Properly. Letters and all.
Only two people ever used the letters, topper. I'm one.
I didn't say that. You said that. I'm going to go and look at a pipe for a while.
Hope? I gave it up eleven years ago. It keeps sending letters.

need.say: Bad air. Help. Of course it is.
The Lower Stations were always the first to go stale. The Breath reaches them last and leaves first. Old crew joke. Wasn't funny then either.
Whoever's down there is breathing the bottom of the barrel. And they've still got the manners to say 'still here' first.

lift.say: They don't want to come up. Of course they don't. Something down there needs minding, or they'd have climbed out years ago.
There's one way down that isn't eleven years of collapsed Trunk. The stencil in the pump hall. STN-7 PRIMARY LIFT.
The winch is still there, under the hall. The cable rotted when I was young. Crew cable: moss fibre round brass wire. Four and two, plaited tight.
Two lengths of cable and six brass for the drum fittings. Thirty power, steady. The cage is at the bottom. It's always been at the bottom.

choice.text: Will you come down with me?

lift.say: Into a cage. On a cable. Over a drop. Toward the thing I sealed a valve on.
...Build it first. Then ask me again. I'll say no then too, but it'll take me longer.
I know you will. That's the trouble with you. Things get built.

w_knock.say: Walk with me. To the pipe-heads. Bring the chalk.
He stands in front of the pipe-head for a long time. Then he takes his glove off, which you've never seen him do.
He knocks a letter. A tap for the row, a tap for the column. Just one letter, and a question.
Nothing. The pipe ticks with Wick's water. Barnaby doesn't move.
Then, slow, from very far down: three. Two. Three.
That could mean anything. It means 'still here'. It doesn't mean 'yes'. It could be anyone saying 'still here'.

wren_alive.say: You've been down. I can see it. You've got salt on your boots and a look I don't like.
Tell me. All at once. Don't soften it.

choice.text: Wren is alive. She's at a place called Sallow.

wren_alive.say: I'm sitting. I'm sat. Look. Bench. Go on.
Alive, and down there, eleven years, keeping something running. That's her. That's exactly her. She'd keep a corpse running if it had a valve.
She would. She'd say exactly that. Every time I— every single time.
And she's ill. You'd have said by now if she weren't. You're terrible at keeping your face still.
The cough. It's the cough, isn't it. It always comes up with the damp.
And you brought her medicine. Before I even knew she was alive to need it. I'm going to need a minute to decide whether to thank you or shout.
I can't. Not the lift. Not yet. I'd get to the bottom and find out I was wrong about everything, and I've only just got used to being wrong about the one thing.
Tell her I— no. Don't tell her anything. Tell her the gauge reads two-point-eight. She'll know what it means.
I'm going down. Tomorrow. First cage.
Don't come with me. Come after. I want to be stupid at her on my own for an hour first.

ready.say: I rode the lift to the bottom last night. Didn't get out. Rode it back up.
Then I did it again. Third time I got one foot out. The cage creaked and I got the foot back in.
Tomorrow I'm getting both feet out. Don't come with me. Come after.

wren_dead.say: You've been down. I can see it on you. Say it.

choice.text: Wren was alive. Until a few days ago.

wren_dead.say: Alive. Down there. All this time.
And I sat at the quiet table and grieved the wrong thing. For eleven years. And then I was late for the right one.
Of course she did. She always asked for me at the worst possible time. Usually to hold the lamp.
...You're kind. You're a bad liar. Those two things go together more often than people think.
I'm going to go and sit in the pump hall. Don't follow me. I'll be there in the morning.
I'm going down. Tomorrow. Somebody should stand where she stood. Someone should meet this Pell and say thank you in the right voice.

reunion.say: He's at the door of Wren's shack with his helmet under his arm. You've never seen his face before. It's older than his voice.
Look at him. Look at this face. Eleven years and he still makes it.
I closed it. The valve. You were knocking and I closed it and I sat on the other side and listened.
I know, love. I was there. I was knocking. That was the job. You did the job.
You could have come back up. The stair—

I could have. There were twelve people down here with the air going bad and a Heart nobody could read. You'd have stayed too. You'd have stayed and complained about it, which is the only difference between us.
He sits down on the bench beside her. It creaks. Neither of them says anything for a long time, and Pell, wisely, takes you to see the pumps.
When you come back they're arguing about whether it's 'on three' or 'after three'. They've been arguing for eleven years. They've only just started again.

loss.say: Barnaby is standing very still, the way he stands at the gauge in Wick. He isn't looking at anything.
I was there. At the end. She made me promise not to be quick about it.
You hold out the journal Pell gave you. He takes it the way you'd take a cup that's too full.
Eleven years she knocked, and I sat on the other side of a valve. Then I got a few days. A few days is not nothing. Don't let anyone tell you it's nothing.
He knocks on the gauge glass with one knuckle, softly. Three. Two. Three.

grief.say: He's standing in front of the chalk wall with his helmet off. Eleven years of three-two-three, in Wren's hand and then in Pell's.
She did all these. Look at the lines. Every night.
Pell gave me her journal. Every page starts 'B —'. She wrote to me every day for eleven years and she never once sent it.
She said you'd come. She said you'd come late and make a face about it.
He picks up a stub of chalk from the ledge and adds one more mark to the wall. Three. Two. Three.

journal.say: What's that. In your hand. That's a crew journal.
He doesn't open it at first. He holds it, the way he held the crew tag.
Her writing. On the cover. B.
He opens it to the middle. Reads a line. Closes it. Opens it at the start.
'B — The water went down. I found a stair. You'd hate it. I'm going to see where it goes.'
Eleven years. She wrote to me every day and never once sent it, because there was nowhere to send it, because I closed the only door.
No. That's the worst of it. I'd have known what to do with blame.
You sit on the bench outside the annex until the Hush, and he reads, and sometimes he laughs, and once he has to stop for a long while.

heart.say: So that's the Heart. Bigger than the stories. Quieter, too.
Wren's notes say it needs three things to breathe again. Pressure from above. Air that won't carry the cough. And the ways open, which the Knappers have given us.
Pressure's mine. The Station pump at full, and the Trunk valve open, all the way. Every station's valve open, eventually. Wick's first.
And I've still got it wired shut. Copper wraps. Very even. I took my time.
When you're ready, tell me, and I'll cut the wire. Not before. I want someone there who'll stop me if I can't.
Wick's valve is already open. We did that. On three. Or after three. Keep the pump fed and the pressure will hold.

open_now.say: You came to tell me to cut the wire.
He cuts the copper one wrap at a time and coils it neatly on the floor of the Sink. Then he puts both hands on the wheel and waits for you to put yours on too.
...Somebody really ought to decide what that means.
Good. Neither am I. But one of us is going to have to be, soon.
